demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
**Case Vignette: Thomas**

Thomas is a 62-year-old married man, a potter by trade, who has been coming to therapy at his wife’s urging. He presents as a sturdy man, with hands that are perpetually stained with clay, and a stillness in his posture that seems more like a held breath than calm. He speaks slowly, often pausing to stare at the floor.

The story he tells begins eighteen months ago, on a Thursday afternoon. He was in his studio, a converted garage behind the house, throwing a large stoneware vase on his wheel. His son, Mark, then 34, was a carpenter. He often stopped by after work, smelling of sawdust and cedar. That day, the phone rang. It was his daughter-in-law. Her voice was a thin, frayed wire. There had been an accident at a job site. A scaffolding collapse. Mark was gone. Thomas remembers the phone slipping from his hand, the wet clay on his receiver, the way the world seemed to go silent, then roar back with the sound of his own blood in his ears.

In the months that followed, Thomas did not stop working. In fact, he worked more. He found that the centering of the clay on the wheel was the only thing that kept his hands from shaking. But the studio is no longer a sanctuary. The smell of damp earth now makes him nauseous. The rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* of the wheel as he kicks it into motion sounds, to him, like a heart beating out of a chest. He cannot listen to the radio anymore; the casual music and chatter feel like an insult to the silence that has settled in his home.

He has not been able to throw a single vase since the day Mark died. Instead, he makes mugs. Dozens and dozens of identical, functional mugs. He says it’s because they are simple, but his wife, Ellen, notes he never gives them away. They sit in boxes in the garage, a silent, growing army of grief. When he tries to make anything more complex, his mind goes blank, or worse, it fills with a single, looping image: the phone on the floor, the clay on the receiver.

The world has become a place of ambushes. A whiff of sawdust from a neighbor’s renovation project on a Sunday morning will stop him cold. He will stand frozen in his own kitchen, his heart hammering against his ribs, until the smell fades. He avoids driving past hardware stores. He has not been able to visit his son’s grave, because the cemetery is near a construction site, and he cannot bear the sound of a nail gun.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies rigid in bed, listening to Ellen breathe, terrified that if he closes his eyes, he will see the phone again, or worse, that he will see Mark’s face in that final, unknowable moment. He has not cried once since the funeral. He feels a pressure behind his eyes, a hot, constricting band around his chest, but the tears will not come. He says he feels like a piece of clay that has been left out too long—hard, cracked, and beyond the point of being reclaimed.

His marriage is strained. Ellen wants to talk about Mark, to share memories. Thomas cannot. He says that remembering the good times feels like a betrayal of the horror of how it ended. He feels constantly on edge, irritable. Last week, a young delivery driver rang the doorbell too long, and Thomas found himself shouting at the man, his face red, his fists clenched, before he knew what he was doing. The rage is new, and it frightens him.

He is a man living in a perpetual state of waiting—for the next smell, the next sound, the next image that will shatter the fragile, functional shell he has built around himself. He has come to therapy not to heal, but because Ellen is afraid of the quiet, and he is afraid of what might happen if he ever allows himself to truly feel the weight of the vase that will never be finished.
